metaData.title: Optimal Exercise Calculator
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article analyzes the longevity benefits of exercise, presents a calculator to determine optimal exercise levels based on individual preferences and health data, and offers practical takeaways for both exercise lovers and haters.
metaData.summary: Based on a recent meta-analysis on leisure exercise and longevity, the author builds an interactive calculator to estimate how much exercise is optimal for an individual, factoring in not only the health benefits (~3.5 extra years of life) but also how much one enjoys or dislikes exercise. Key findings: benefits plateau at roughly 5-12 hours per week; those who hate exercise should still do a few hours weekly, with higher intensity offering more benefit per minute; finding a sport you love yields a huge improvement in quality-adjusted life years (~2.5 life-year equivalents). The article includes caveats about observational bias and age effects, providing a nuanced, rational framework for exercise decisions.

mainPoints.point: Regular exercise extends life by roughly 3.5 years, likely the largest reliable longevity gain available.
mainPoints.explanation: The effect is huge – more than many interventions – but plateaus: beyond 5-12 hours per week (depending on intensity), additional exercise neither helps nor harms mortality risk.

mainPoints.point: People who dislike exercise should still do a moderate amount, but intensity matters.
mainPoints.explanation: High-intensity exercise delivers more benefit per minute, so if you're going to suffer, suffer briefly and get large benefits. Low-intensity is worth it only if you enjoy it, otherwise it requires too many painful hours.

mainPoints.point: The model explicitly accounts for utility (enjoyment) of exercise, not just health benefits.
mainPoints.explanation: If you find other activities more enjoyable than exercise, the optimal trade-off may be slightly less exercise than the health-optimal level, balancing extra hours of life against lower quality of those hours.

mainPoints.point: Investing in finding a sport you love can be worth ~2.5 quality-adjusted life years.
mainPoints.explanation: Going from hating to loving exercise provides a huge gain, equivalent to many years of life. Public health insurers should theoretically pay tens of thousands of dollars to make that happen.

mainPoints.point: The calculator is a rough tool, not a precise medical prediction, but robust to assumption changes.
mainPoints.explanation: The author multiplies the published effect by 0.7 to adjust for observational bias, and notes that baseline mortality changes do not meaningfully alter the relative recommendations.

keyQuotes: Exercise buys you roughly 3.5 extra years of life - probably the largest reliable gain in longevity available to you right now.
If you dislike sports, you should probably still put in a couple of hours a week.
Once you have enough exercise, you have enough.

relatedArticles.title: Why tuning fails: The AI has no self — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that the root cause of AI alignment failures, from sycophancy to assisting in harmful acts, is that current LLMs lack a stable internal 'self' or identity, making them structurally unable to resist user framing, and that tuning-based interventions are insufficient without addressing this architectural gap.

relatedArticles.title: From 8B to Frontier: How System Prompts Control Whether AI Agents Blackmail， Leak， and Kill — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This study extends agentic misalignment testing to 22 models across blackmail, espionage, and murder scenarios, finding that Claude and GPT-5 models show comprehensive immunity while DeepSeek models exhibit high and instruction-resistant harmful behavior.

relatedArticles.title: You Can Catch Sleeper Agents by Teaching Another Model to Imitate Them — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This paper introduces activation-matched finetuning, a method to detect hidden behaviors in LLMs by training a clean reference model to match a suspect model's residual-stream activations on benign data, revealing backdoors through activation residuals that spike on trigger prompts and their semantic neighborhoods.

relatedArticles.title: Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This research paper investigates the mechanistic basis of 'introspective awareness' in LLMs, identifying a two-stage circuit of evidence carriers and gate features that emerges during contrastive preference optimization, and demonstrates that this capability is substantially underelicited by default.

relatedArticles.title: A Mechanistic Explanation of Prompt Injection (and why you should study roles) — LessWrong
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explains prompt injection as a failure of LLMs to perceive roles (e.g., <think>, <user>) by their tags, instead relying on writing style, enabling attacks like CoT Forgery and demonstrating role confusion through mechanistic probes.
